claims.text: A hybrid machine-learning interatomic-potential and quasi-harmonic method can compute both solid and liquid free energies near fusion with fidelity comparable to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The hybrid method can substantially reduce computational cost relative to full ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations.
Accurate near-fusion calculations require DFT-level vibrational and electronic entropy treatment in both solid and liquid states.
ML interatomic potentials can be used to sample atomic configurations in place of most explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Quasi-harmonic corrections can capture the vibrational free energy of ordered solid phases.
Targeted, minimal molecular-dynamics sampling in the fluid can correct its anharmonic free-energy contribution.
The method is applicable from 0.7 to 1.1 times the fusion temperature.
The method can be extended from elemental and binary metals to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
DFT-trained ML potentials can reproduce energies and forces with near-DFT accuracy in elemental and multicomponent systems.
ML potentials offer a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost.
Vibrational and electronic free-energy terms can be represented through reduced thermodynamic models.
Combining ML sampling, quasi-harmonic free energies, and limited melt corrections retains the key entropy contributions needed for fusion calculations.
The hybrid method should predict solid-liquid free-energy differences and fusion temperatures close to ab initio molecular-dynamics benchmarks.
The hybrid method should reduce computational cost by at least approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The hybrid method should be significantly faster than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD provide high-fidelity but computationally expensive free-energy evaluations.
The method is expected to remain valid only when adequate DFT training data are available and solid-state anharmonicity is not extreme.
Strong electron-vibration coupling or pronounced melt anharmonicity will increase uncertainty.
Errors greater than 10 meV/atom in phase free-energy differences or 50 K in melting temperature relative to ab initio benchmarks would falsify the fidelity claim.
Failure to achieve at least a tenfold cost saving over TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems would falsify the cost claim.

contradictions.description: The initial state calls for full DFT-level vibrational and electronic entropy treatment in both phases, whereas the intervention replaces that treatment with quasi-harmonic models and only limited corrections; the hypothesis does not clearly reconcile approximation with the stated full-DFT requirement.

The benchmark design specifies elemental and binary systems, but the cost falsification rule requires a comparison against TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems, which is not included explicitly in the stated benchmark set.
